topics.title: Cells and microscopes
topics.intro: Every living thing is built from cells. With a light microscope you can see the nucleus and the cell wall; an electron microscope shows far smaller parts, like ribosomes.
topics.teach: Explain three differences between a plant cell and an animal cell, and what each extra part does.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to explain how a microscope’s magnification is worked out.
topics.hook: Animal cells have the basic kit; plant cells add three extras: a **wall**, a **vacuole** and **chloroplasts**.

topics.title: Specialised cells, organs and digestion
topics.intro: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems. In digestion, enzymes act like molecular scissors, breaking big food molecules into small ones the blood can absorb.
topics.teach: Explain the job of an enzyme, using amylase as an example, and why boiling stops it working.
topics.talk: At dinner, ask {him} which nutrients in the meal will be broken down by which enzymes.
topics.hook: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism; enzymes are the **scissors** that cut food small.

topics.title: Breathing and respiration
topics.intro: Breathing moves air in and out; respiration is the chemical reaction in every cell that releases energy from glucose. They are not the same thing!
topics.teach: Explain the difference between breathing and respiration, and write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
topics.talk: After a sprint, ask {him} why {she} is panting even after stopping (oxygen debt).
topics.hook: Breathing **moves air**; respiration **releases energy**, in every living cell, day and night.

topics.title: Photosynthesis and plants
topics.intro: Plants make their own food: in chloroplasts, light energy turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Almost every food chain on Earth starts here.
topics.teach: Explain the word equation for photosynthesis and three things that could limit its rate.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why a plant left in a dark cupboard turns yellow and dies.
topics.hook: Photo = **light**, synthesis = **putting together** (Greek): plants use light to build glucose.

topics.title: Ecosystems and food webs
topics.intro: In an ecosystem every organism depends on others. Energy flows along food chains, but most is lost at each step, which is why there are few top predators.
topics.teach: Explain what would happen to a food web if one species disappeared, using a real example.
topics.talk: On a walk, ask {him} to build a food chain from what you can see.
topics.hook: Energy flows along the chain, and only about a **tenth** passes up each step.

topics.title: DNA, variation and evolution
topics.intro: DNA in the nucleus carries the genetic code, arranged in genes on chromosomes. Variation, plus natural selection over many generations, explains how species evolve.
topics.teach: Explain natural selection using the peppered moth or antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which of {her} features are inherited, which are environmental, and which are both.
topics.hook: Nucleus = **library**, chromosome = **book**, gene = **recipe**, base = **letter**.

topics.title: Health, microbes and disease
topics.intro: Bacteria, viruses and fungi can cause disease. Our bodies fight back with white blood cells; vaccines train the immune system in advance. Hippocrates, the Greek “father of medicine”, insisted that diseases have natural causes.
topics.teach: Explain how a vaccine protects you without making you ill.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why antibiotics do not work against a cold.
topics.hook: Antibiotics kill **bacteria**, never viruses; vaccines **train** the immune system before the fight.

topics.title: Particles, states and density
topics.intro: Democritus, in ancient Greece, guessed that everything is made of tiny uncuttable pieces: atomos. The particle model explains solids, liquids and gases, diffusion and density.
topics.teach: Explain, using particles, why a gas fills its container and a solid keeps its shape.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why you can smell perfume across a room (diffusion).
topics.hook: Solids **vibrate**, liquids **slide**, gases **zoom**, and the particles themselves never change size.

topics.title: Elements, compounds and separating mixtures
topics.intro: An element has one type of atom; a compound has different atoms chemically bonded; a mixture is not chemically joined, so it can be separated by filtering, evaporating, distilling or chromatography.
topics.teach: Explain how you would get pure water and pure salt back from salty water.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether air, water and gold are elements, compounds or mixtures.
topics.hook: Element: one kind of atom. Compound: different atoms **bonded**. Mixture: **not joined**, so it can be separated.

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.intro: Mendeleev arranged the elements so that ones with similar properties line up in columns called groups. He left gaps for elements nobody had found yet, and was proved right.
topics.teach: Explain why the elements in Group 1 react in similar ways, and why reactivity increases down the group.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to name a metal and a non-metal and give one property of each.
topics.hook: Columns are **groups** (similar properties); rows are **periods**.

topics.title: Chemical reactions and equations
topics.intro: In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged into new substances: no atoms are made or destroyed, so mass is conserved. Combustion, oxidation and thermal decomposition are common types.
topics.teach: Explain how you can tell a chemical change from a physical change, with two signs of a reaction.
topics.talk: Light a candle together and ask {him} what is being made as the wax burns.
topics.hook: Atoms are never made or destroyed, only **rearranged**: mass in = mass out.

topics.title: Acids, alkalis and metals
topics.intro: Acids have a pH below 7, alkalis above 7. Acid + alkali → salt + water (neutralisation). Metals react with acids to make a salt and hydrogen, and the reactivity series ranks how readily they react.
topics.teach: Explain the reactivity series and how it explains why gold is found pure in the ground but iron is not.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why indigestion tablets work.
topics.hook: **MASH**: **M**etal + **A**cid → **S**alt + **H**ydrogen. Acid + alkali → salt + water.

topics.title: The Earth and its atmosphere
topics.intro: Rocks are recycled over millions of years in the rock cycle; carbon is recycled between air, living things, oceans and rocks. Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide faster than it is removed.
topics.teach: Explain how burning fossil fuels contributes to climate change, using the carbon cycle.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which rock type a fossil is most likely to be found in, and why.
topics.hook: **Igneous** from fire (Latin ignis), **sedimentary** from layers, **metamorphic** from change.

topics.title: Forces, motion and pressure
topics.intro: Forces change an object’s speed, direction or shape. Balanced forces mean constant speed; unbalanced forces mean acceleration. Pressure is force spread over an area; a moment is a turning effect.
topics.teach: Explain why a skydiver reaches a terminal velocity.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why snowshoes stop you sinking into snow.
topics.hook: Balanced forces: **no change** in motion. Unbalanced forces: speed up, slow down or turn.

topics.title: Energy, power and efficiency
topics.intro: Energy is stored (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear…) and transferred by forces, heating, electricity and waves. It is never used up, but some is always wasted, usually as heat.
topics.teach: Explain the energy transfers when a ball is dropped and bounces lower each time.
topics.talk: Check the power rating on the kettle and ask {him} how much a boil costs.
topics.hook: Energy is never used up, only **shifted between stores**, and some always leaks away as heat.

topics.title: Electricity and magnetism
topics.intro: Current is the flow of charge; potential difference is the push; resistance opposes the flow. In series, current is the same everywhere; in parallel, current splits. A current also makes a magnetic field.
topics.teach: Explain what happens to the brightness of bulbs when you add more in series, and why.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why lights in a house are wired in parallel, not series.
topics.hook: Series: one loop, **current the same** everywhere. Parallel: branches, **current splits**.

topics.title: Sound and light
topics.intro: Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium; light is a transverse wave that can cross empty space at 300 000 km per second. Both reflect and refract.
topics.teach: Explain why you see lightning before you hear thunder.
topics.talk: Put a pencil in a glass of water and ask {him} to explain why it looks bent.
topics.hook: Sound needs **particles** to pass it on; light can cross **empty space**, almost a million times faster.

topics.title: Space, gravity and the seasons
topics.intro: Gravity holds moons around planets and planets around the Sun. The seasons happen because the Earth’s axis is tilted, not because we are nearer the Sun. Eratosthenes measured the Earth’s size more than 2000 years ago using shadows.
topics.teach: Explain why it is summer in Britain when the Earth is actually furthest from the Sun.
topics.talk: Look for the Moon together and ask {him} what phase it is in and why.
topics.hook: Seasons come from the **tilt**, not the distance: the Earth is closest to the Sun in January.

topics.title: Working scientifically
topics.intro: Good science is about fair tests, careful measurement and honest conclusions. Know your variables, and the difference between accurate, precise and repeatable results.
topics.teach: Explain the independent, dependent and control variables in an experiment of your choice.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to design a fair test to find the best paper for a paper aeroplane.
topics.hook: **Cows Moo Softly**: **C**hange one thing, **M**easure one thing, keep everything else the **S**ame.

topics.title: Inside the atom: isotopes and bonding
topics.intro: Atoms have a tiny nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around it. Atoms bond by transferring electrons (ionic) or sharing them (covalent).
topics.teach: Explain the difference between ionic and covalent bonding with an example of each.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what carbon-12 and carbon-14 have in common, and what is different.
topics.hook: **P**rotons **p**ositive, **n**eutrons **n**eutral, both in the nucleus; electrons whizz round in shells.

topics.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
topics.intro: Visible light is only a small part of a family of waves, from radio to gamma rays, all travelling at the speed of light. Shorter wavelengths carry more energy.
topics.teach: Explain why X-rays are useful but dangerous.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which electromagnetic waves {she} used today (radio, microwaves, visible light…).
topics.hook: **R**aging **M**artians **I**nvaded **V**enus **U**sing **X**-ray **G**uns: radio to gamma.

topics.title: Genetics and Punnett squares
topics.intro: Genes come in different versions called alleles. Dominant alleles show up even with just one copy; recessive ones only when both copies match. Punnett squares predict the chances.
topics.teach: Explain why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child (using a simplified model).
topics.talk: Ask {him} to draw a Punnett square for two parents who are both Bb.
topics.hook: A **capital** letter (dominant) shows with one copy; a **small** letter (recessive) needs two.

items.explain: The nucleus contains DNA and controls the cell.
items.hook: The nucleus is the cell’s **control centre**, holding the DNA instructions.

items.explain: The membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
items.hook: The membrane is the **gatekeeper**: it decides what gets in and out.

items.explain: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration releases energy.
items.hook: Mitochondria are the **powerhouses** of the cell, where aerobic respiration releases energy.
items.example: Muscle cells, which need lots of energy, are packed with mitochondria.

items.explain: Ribosomes make proteins. They are too small to see with a light microscope.
items.hook: Ribosomes are tiny **protein factories**, too small for a light microscope to show.

items.explain: The cellulose cell wall supports and strengthens a plant cell.
items.hook: The cell **wall** is like the walls of a house: rigid **cellulose** support.
items.example: The crunch of fresh celery comes from firm plant cell walls.

items.explain: The permanent vacuole is filled with cell sap and keeps the cell firm.
items.hook: A full vacuole keeps the cell firm, like air in a bouncy castle.
items.example: A limp lettuce leaf crisps up in cold water as its vacuoles fill again.

items.explain: Chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll, which absorbs light for photosynthesis.
items.hook: Chloro- means **green** (Greek chlōros): chloroplasts hold green chlorophyll.
items.example: Leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green.

items.prompt: Which part is found in plant cells but NEVER in animal cells?

options.text: Chloroplasts
Mitochondria
options.feedback: Both plant and animal cells have mitochondria: both respire.

options.text: Nucleus
options.feedback: Both have a nucleus.

options.text: Cell membrane
options.feedback: Both have a membrane; plants have a wall as well.

items.explain: Plant cells have three extras: a cell wall, a permanent vacuole and chloroplasts.
items.hook: Plant extras: **wall, vacuole, chloroplasts**. Both have mitochondria, because both respire.

items.prompt: How is a bacterial cell different from an animal cell?

options.text: It has no nucleus; its DNA is loose
It is far bigger than an animal cell
options.feedback: Bacteria are usually much smaller than animal cells.

options.text: It has chloroplasts for photosynthesis
options.feedback: Bacteria never have chloroplasts (a few, like cyanobacteria, photosynthesise without them).

items.explain: It has no nucleus: its DNA floats in the cytoplasm. Bacteria are prokaryotes: no nucleus, and often a loop of DNA plus small rings called plasmids.
items.hook: Pro-karyote = “before the kernel” (Greek): bacteria have **no nucleus**.
items.example: The bacteria in live yoghurt are single prokaryotic cells.

items.prompt: Why do you add a stain such as iodine when preparing an onion cell slide?

options.text: To make the cell parts show up
To kill the cells so they keep still
options.feedback: The point is contrast: cell parts are almost transparent.

options.text: To make the cells swell up bigger
options.feedback: Stains don’t change size.

items.explain: To make the parts of the cell easier to see. Most cell parts are colourless; stains colour them so they show up.
items.hook: Stains add **contrast**: colourless cell parts suddenly show up.

items.prompt: Which kind of microscope can show ribosomes and the inside of mitochondria?
items.explain: Electron microscopes have far higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes.
items.hook: Electron microscopes use beams of **electrons**, not light, so they show far tinier details.
items.example: Coronaviruses are named after the crown of spikes scientists saw round them using electron microscopes.

items.hook: **I AM** triangle: **I**mage size = **A**ctual size × **M**agnification.

items.prompt: Put these in order, from smallest to largest.
items.explain: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs work together in organ systems, and those make up the organism.
items.hook: Smallest to largest: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism, each built from the one before.
items.example: Muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → you.

items.prompt: Why does a sperm cell have lots of mitochondria?

options.text: To release energy for swimming
To provide food for the growing egg
options.feedback: The mitochondria power the sperm itself.

options.text: To store energy for the baby later
options.feedback: That is the egg’s job, which is why eggs are large.

items.explain: To release energy for swimming with its tail. Specialised cells have features suited to their job: sperm need energy to swim.
items.hook: Lots of swimming needs lots of energy, so lots of **mitochondria**.

items.prompt: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?

options.text: To leave more room for haemoglobin
So that they can divide more quickly
options.feedback: Without a nucleus they cannot divide at all.

options.text: Because they are dead before they work
options.feedback: They are living, specialised cells.

items.explain: To make more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen. Their biconcave shape and lack of nucleus help them carry as much oxygen as possible.
items.hook: No nucleus = more room for **haemoglobin**, the oxygen carrier.
items.example: Blood is red because of the iron-containing haemoglobin in red blood cells.

items.prompt: What does an enzyme do in digestion?

options.text: Speeds up breaking big food molecules into small ones
Absorbs the digested food into the blood
options.feedback: Absorption happens through the small intestine wall.

options.text: Joins small molecules into bigger, longer-lasting ones
options.feedback: The opposite: digestion makes molecules small enough to absorb.

items.explain: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they speed up reactions without being used up.
items.hook: Enzymes are **molecular scissors**, cutting big food molecules into small ones.
items.example: Biological washing powders use enzymes to digest food stains on clothes.

items.prompt: Which enzyme, found in saliva, breaks starch into sugars?
items.explain: Chew bread for a long time and it starts to taste sweet: amylase at work.
items.hook: **Amyl**- comes from amylum, Latin for **starch**; -ase means an enzyme.
items.example: Chew a plain cracker for a minute and it starts to taste sweet.

items.prompt: Which type of enzyme breaks proteins into amino acids?
items.explain: Proteases work in the stomach (pepsin) and small intestine.
items.hook: **Prot**ease breaks down **prot**eins.
items.example: Meat tenderisers contain protease enzymes from papaya or pineapple.

items.prompt: Which type of enzyme breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol?
items.explain: Bile from the liver breaks fat into droplets so lipase can work faster.
items.hook: **Lip**ase breaks down **lip**ids (fats and oils).
items.example: Some biological washing powders contain lipase to lift greasy stains.

items.prompt: Why is the small intestine lined with millions of tiny villi?

options.text: They give a huge surface area for absorption
They grind the food up into smaller pieces
options.feedback: Teeth do the chewing.

options.text: They make the stomach acid that kills microbes
options.feedback: Acid is made in the stomach.

items.explain: Villi have thin walls and a good blood supply, so small molecules diffuse into the blood quickly.
items.hook: Villi are like the loops on a **towel**: lots of folds give a huge surface to soak things up.

items.prompt: Why does boiling stop an enzyme working?

options.text: Heat changes the active site’s shape (denatured)
It kills the enzyme, because enzymes are alive
options.feedback: Enzymes are proteins, not living things.

options.text: The heat dissolves the enzyme in the water
options.feedback: The enzyme is still there, but its shape is ruined.

items.explain: The heat changes the shape of its active site, so it is denatured. Enzymes work by shape: the substrate fits the active site like a key in a lock. Too much heat and the lock is bent.
items.hook: Lock and key: heat **bends the lock**, so the key no longer fits.
items.example: A boiled egg white can never turn clear and runny again: its proteins are denatured.

items.prompt: Why is there hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
items.answer: it kills microbes and helps enzymes
distractors: it digests the fat in food
it absorbs water into the blood
it makes bile to emulsify fats
items.explain: It kills microbes and helps stomach enzymes work. Stomach protease (pepsin) works best in acid conditions.
items.hook: Stomach acid is a **microbe killer**, and pepsin likes it acidic.
items.example: Heartburn is stomach acid escaping up into the gullet.

items.prompt: Complete the word equation for aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → … + water (+ energy released)
items.explain: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. It happens in the mitochondria.
items.hook: Respiration is photosynthesis **backwards**: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
items.example: Breathe out through limewater and it turns milky: the carbon dioxide comes from respiration.

items.prompt: What is the difference between breathing and respiration?

options.text: Breathing moves air; respiration releases energy in cells
They are two names for exactly the same process
options.feedback: A common mix-up: respiration happens in every cell, even in plants.

options.text: Respiration only happens in the lungs, breathing everywhere
options.feedback: It happens in every living cell.

items.explain: Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs; respiration is a chemical reaction in cells. Plants respire too, day and night, even though they don’t breathe.
items.hook: **B**reathing is the **b**ellows; **r**espiration is the **r**eaction in cells.

items.prompt: In muscles short of oxygen, glucose is turned into… (anaerobic respiration)
items.explain: Lactic acid builds up during hard exercise; you pay back the “oxygen debt” by panting afterwards.
items.hook: An-aerobic = **without air** (Greek): short of oxygen, muscles make lactic acid.
items.example: After a 100 m sprint you keep panting to pay back the oxygen debt.

items.prompt: When yeast respires anaerobically it makes ethanol and which gas, which makes bread rise?
items.explain: This is fermentation, used in baking and brewing.
items.hook: Yeast **ferments** sugar: ethanol + carbon dioxide.
items.example: The holes in a slice of bread are bubbles of carbon dioxide made by yeast.

items.prompt: How are the alveoli in the lungs suited to gas exchange?

options.text: Huge surface area, thin walls, rich blood supply
Thick, strong walls to stop them bursting
options.feedback: Thin walls give a short distance for diffusion.

options.text: They are coated in mucus to trap the oxygen
options.feedback: Mucus is in the airways to trap dust and microbes.

items.explain: Huge surface area, walls one cell thick, and a rich blood supply. Oxygen diffuses into the blood, and carbon dioxide out, across very thin walls.
items.hook: Alveoli are tiny **air sacs**, like bunches of grapes, with walls one cell thick.

items.prompt: Why do smokers often get breathless?

options.text: Smoke damages the alveoli and carbon monoxide cuts oxygen carried
Smoke makes the lungs grow bigger, so they need more air
options.feedback: Smoking damages the lungs; it does not enlarge them usefully.

options.text: Nicotine uses up the oxygen in the blood as it is digested
options.feedback: Nicotine is an addictive drug, not oxygen.

items.explain: Tar and smoke damage the alveoli and cilia, and carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen blood can carry. Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin more strongly than oxygen does.
items.hook: Carbon monoxide **hijacks haemoglobin**, so the blood carries less oxygen.
items.example: Homes have carbon monoxide alarms because the gas has no colour or smell.

items.prompt: Put the route of air into the body in order.
items.explain: Air goes down the trachea (windpipe), into a bronchus, through ever smaller bronchioles, to the alveoli.
items.hook: Nose → trachea → bronchus → bronchiole → alveolus: big pipes branching into ever tinier ones.
items.example: The branching airways are called the bronchial tree: an upside-down tree in your chest.

items.prompt: Where in the cell does aerobic respiration take place?

options.text: Mitochondria
Nucleus
options.feedback: The nucleus holds DNA.

options.text: Chloroplasts
options.feedback: Chloroplasts do photosynthesis.

items.explain: Muscle cells have lots of mitochondria because they need lots of energy.
items.hook: Mitochondria are the cell’s **power stations**: aerobic respiration happens there.

items.prompt: Complete the word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + … (using light energy)
items.explain: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, using light absorbed by chlorophyll.
items.hook: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen: the reverse of respiration.
items.example: Pondweed in bright light gives off streams of tiny oxygen bubbles.

items.prompt: Which of these does NOT limit the rate of photosynthesis?

options.text: Oxygen in the air
Light intensity
options.feedback: More light means faster photosynthesis, up to a point.

options.text: Carbon dioxide concentration
options.feedback: CO₂ is a raw material, so it can limit the rate.

options.text: Temperature around the plant
options.feedback: Enzymes control photosynthesis, so temperature matters.

items.explain: The amount of oxygen in the air. Light, CO₂ and temperature are the limiting factors. Oxygen is a product.
items.hook: The limiting factors are **light, CO₂ and temperature**: the one in shortest supply sets the pace.
items.example: Growers pump extra carbon dioxide into greenhouses to make tomatoes grow faster.

items.prompt: A leaf is tested with iodine and turns blue-black. What does that show?

options.text: Starch is present: it has photosynthesised
The leaf contains protein from the soil
options.feedback: Biuret tests for protein; iodine tests for starch.

options.text: The leaf is dead and has stopped working
options.feedback: It shows starch, made from the glucose of photosynthesis.

items.explain: Starch is present, so the leaf has been photosynthesising. Plants store glucose as starch. Variegated leaves only go blue-black in the green parts.
items.hook: Iodine: orange-brown → **blue-black** means **starch**.
items.example: A drop of iodine on a cut potato turns blue-black.

items.prompt: What are stomata?

options.text: Tiny holes in leaves that let gases in and out
The tubes in roots that carry water upwards
options.feedback: Those are xylem vessels.

options.text: The green parts of a cell that trap light
options.feedback: Those are chloroplasts.

items.explain: Tiny holes, mostly under the leaf, that let gases in and out. Guard cells open and close the stomata; carbon dioxide enters and water vapour escapes.
items.hook: Stoma is Greek for **mouth**: stomata are the leaf’s tiny mouths.

items.prompt: Which tubes carry water up from the roots to the leaves?
items.explain: Xylem carries water up; phloem carries dissolved sugars around the plant.
items.hook: **Ph**loem carries **f**ood (both start with an f sound), so xylem is the water pipe.
items.example: Stand a celery stick in food colouring and its xylem vessels turn coloured.

items.prompt: Root hair cells take in water by osmosis. What else do they absorb from the soil?
items.explain: Plants need minerals such as nitrates (for proteins) and magnesium (for chlorophyll).
items.hook: Root hairs soak up water **and minerals**, such as nitrates and magnesium.
items.example: Garden “plant food” is mostly mineral ions, such as nitrates.

items.explain: The sticky stigma catches pollen.
items.hook: The **st**igma is **st**icky, to catch pollen.

items.explain: The anther makes pollen, which contains the male sex cells.
items.hook: The stamen (anther + filament) is the male part: think “sta-**men**”.
items.example: Lily anthers drop orange pollen that stains clothes.

items.explain: The ovary contains ovules; after fertilisation it becomes the fruit.
items.hook: After fertilisation the ovary becomes the **fruit** and the ovules become **seeds**.
items.example: A pea pod is a ripened ovary, and the peas were its ovules.

items.prompt: In the 1600s van Helmont grew a willow tree for five years. It gained 74 kg but the soil lost only about 57 g. Where did most of the tree’s mass come from?

options.text: Carbon dioxide from the air
Minerals from the soil
options.feedback: The soil lost almost nothing: that was the surprise.

options.text: Energy from the sunlight
options.feedback: Light gives energy, not mass.

items.explain: Carbon dioxide from the air (and water). Van Helmont thought it was water. We now know the carbon comes from CO₂ in the air.
items.hook: A tree is built mostly from **thin air**: its carbon comes from CO₂.
items.example: Most of the mass of a log on the fire came from carbon dioxide in the air.

items.prompt: In a food chain, what do the arrows show?

options.text: The direction energy flows, eaten to eater
Who eats whom, pointing at the food eaten
options.feedback: The arrow points TO the animal doing the eating.

options.text: Which animal is the bigger of the two
options.feedback: Size does not matter here.

items.explain: The direction energy flows: from the eaten to the eater. grass → rabbit → fox: energy passes from grass to rabbit to fox.
items.hook: Arrows point to the **eater**: read each arrow as “is eaten by”.
items.example: grass → rabbit → fox: grass is eaten by rabbit, rabbit is eaten by fox.

items.prompt: What is the name for an organism that makes its own food, at the start of a food chain?
items.explain: Producers (plants and algae) photosynthesise.
items.hook: **Producers produce** their own food by photosynthesis.
items.example: Tiny phytoplankton in the sea are the producers at the base of food chains that feed fish and whales.

items.prompt: Why are food chains rarely longer than four or five steps?

options.text: Energy is lost at each step
Top predators would run out of space to hunt
options.feedback: The reason is energy.

options.text: There are not enough species in a habitat
options.feedback: There are millions of species; energy is the limit.

items.explain: Energy is lost at each step, through movement, heat and waste. Only about 10% of the energy passes to the next level, so there is little left for top predators.
items.hook: Only about **10%** passes up each step: the rest goes on movement, heat and waste.
items.example: A field of wheat feeds far more people than the same field used to raise cattle.

items.prompt: Which organisms break down dead material and recycle nutrients into the soil?
items.explain: Bacteria and fungi are decomposers.
items.hook: Decomposers are nature’s **recyclers**.
items.example: A compost heap, mushrooms on a rotting log and mould on old bread are decomposers at work.

items.prompt: Why would a fall in bee numbers worry farmers?

options.text: Many crops need insects to pollinate them
Bees eat the pests that attack the crops
options.feedback: Bees mainly matter as pollinators.

options.text: Bees dig tunnels that make the soil fertile
options.feedback: Worms and decomposers do that.

items.explain: Without pollination, many fruits and seeds never form.
items.hook: Bees are flying **pollen couriers**.
items.example: Apples, strawberries and oilseed rape all crop better when bees visit their flowers.

items.prompt: A pesticide sprayed on plants ends up most concentrated in birds of prey. Why?

options.text: It builds up at each step of the chain
Birds of prey eat the sprayed plants directly
options.feedback: They are at the top of the chain.

options.text: The birds make the pesticide in their own bodies
options.feedback: It comes from the spray.

items.explain: It builds up at each step because animals eat many organisms below them. This is bioaccumulation; DDT harmed eagles and falcons this way.
items.hook: Bio-**accumulation**: poison piles up the chain because each eater eats many meals.
items.example: After pesticides such as DDT were phased out, peregrine falcons recovered in Britain.

items.prompt: In a pond, fish eat water fleas, and water fleas eat algae. If the fish all died, what would most likely happen first?

options.text: Water fleas would rise; algae would fall
Algae would rise; water fleas would fall
options.feedback: More water fleas would eat more algae.

options.text: Nothing would change, because fish are at the top
options.feedback: Every link affects the others.

items.explain: With no predator, the fleas multiply and eat more algae.
items.hook: Remove a predator and its prey **boom**; then the prey’s food **crashes**.
items.example: Where sea otters vanished, sea urchins boomed and ate whole kelp forests.

items.prompt: Animals of the same species competing for food, mates and territory is called…
items.explain: Organisms compete within and between species; plants compete for light, water and minerals.
items.hook: Competition: the same food, space or mates, and not enough to go round.
items.example: Seedlings sown too close together compete for light and stay small.

items.prompt: Put these in order from largest to smallest.
items.explain: The nucleus holds chromosomes; each chromosome is a long DNA molecule containing many genes; genes are made of sequences of bases.
items.hook: Nucleus = library, chromosome = book, gene = recipe, base = letter.

items.prompt: How many chromosomes are there in a normal human body cell?
items.explain: 23 pairs: one of each pair from each parent. Sperm and eggs have 23.
items.hook: **23 pairs** = 46: one of each pair from each parent.
items.example: A sperm and an egg each bring 23 chromosomes: 23 + 23 = 46.

items.prompt: Who used Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray images to build the double helix model of DNA in 1953?
items.explain: Franklin’s “Photo 51” was vital evidence; Maurice Wilkins also worked on it.
items.hook: A double helix is a **twisted ladder**.
items.example: A spiral staircase has the same shape as DNA’s double helix.

items.prompt: Which of these is caused ONLY by the environment?

options.text: A scar
Natural eye colour
options.feedback: Eye colour is inherited.

options.text: Height
options.feedback: Height depends on genes AND environment (such as diet).

items.explain: Scars, language and haircuts are environmental. Many features, like height and weight, depend on both.
items.hook: Genes deal the cards; the **environment** plays them. A scar is all environment.
items.example: Identical twins share their genes, but only one might have a scar.

items.prompt: In industrial Britain, dark peppered moths became more common than pale ones. Why?

options.text: Dark moths were better hidden on sooty trees, so more survived
The moths’ wings turned dark from soot landing on them
options.feedback: Individuals cannot change their genes; the dark ones survived more often.

options.text: Pale moths flew away to cleaner countryside to breed
options.feedback: They were eaten more often.

items.explain: On soot-covered trees, dark moths were better hidden from birds, so more survived to breed. Natural selection: variation, a survival advantage, and passing the useful gene on.
items.hook: Natural selection: **variation**, **survival** of the best suited, **passing on** the genes.
items.example: Since Britain’s air was cleaned up, pale peppered moths have become common again.

items.prompt: Which naturalist published On the Origin of Species in 1859?
items.explain: Darwin’s ideas were shaped by his voyage on HMS Beagle, including the Galápagos Islands.
items.hook: Darwin + the **Beagle** + the **Galápagos** = evolution by natural selection.
items.example: Darwin’s face was on the Bank of England £10 note from 2000 to 2018.

items.prompt: Why is it important to finish a course of antibiotics?

options.text: So no partly resistant bacteria survive
So that it kills any viruses as well
options.feedback: Antibiotics don’t work on viruses.

options.text: Because unused tablets go off in the bottle
options.feedback: The reason is resistance.

items.explain: So no partly resistant bacteria survive to multiply. Resistant bacteria are natural selection happening fast: a big problem for modern medicine.
items.hook: Stop early and the **toughest** bacteria survive and multiply.
items.example: MRSA is a “superbug”: bacteria resistant to many antibiotics.

items.prompt: Which word means a species has no living members left?
items.explain: The dodo has been extinct since the late 1600s.
items.hook: **Dead as a dodo**: extinct means gone for ever.
items.example: The dodo lived only on Mauritius and was wiped out after sailors arrived.

items.prompt: How do fossils support the theory of evolution?

options.text: Older rock layers show simpler forms that change over time
Fossils show that animals have never changed
options.feedback: They show change over very long times.

options.text: Every fossil found is of a species still alive today
options.feedback: Most fossil species are extinct.

items.explain: The fossil record shows how organisms have changed over millions of years.
items.hook: Rock layers are a **history book**: the deeper the page, the older it is.
items.example: The cliffs of Dorset’s Jurassic Coast are full of fossil ammonites.

items.prompt: Why don’t antibiotics cure a cold?

options.text: Colds are viral; antibiotics kill bacteria
Colds are too mild for antibiotics to notice
options.feedback: It is about the type of microbe.

options.text: Colds are caused by fungi, not by bacteria
options.feedback: Colds are viruses.

items.explain: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only kill bacteria. Antibiotics attack parts of bacterial cells, such as their cell walls, which viruses do not have; viruses also reproduce inside our own cells.
items.hook: Anti**b**iotics beat **b**acteria; viruses hide inside your own cells.

items.prompt: How does a vaccine protect you?

options.text: A harmless form of the microbe trains white blood cells
It kills every microbe in your body for a few years
options.feedback: It trains the immune system for one particular disease.

options.text: It is a strong antibiotic that stays in your blood
options.feedback: Vaccines prevent disease; they are not a cure.

items.explain: It contains a harmless form of the microbe, so white blood cells learn to make the right antibodies. Memory cells mean that next time, antibodies are made so fast you don’t fall ill.
items.hook: A vaccine is a **wanted poster**: white blood cells learn the face before the real criminal arrives.
items.example: The MMR jab protects against measles, mumps and rubella.

items.prompt: Who developed the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796?
items.explain: He used cowpox; “vaccine” comes from vacca, Latin for cow.
items.hook: Vacca = **cow** (Latin): Jenner used cowpox to protect against smallpox.
items.example: Smallpox was declared wiped out worldwide in 1980.

items.prompt: Who discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928?
items.explain: He noticed mould killing bacteria on a dish he had left out.
items.hook: Fleming’s messy bench: a mouldy dish led to **penicillin**.
items.example: Penicillin, from the Penicillium mould, has saved millions of lives.

items.prompt: Which ancient Greek doctor, “the father of medicine”, taught that illness has natural causes, not punishment by the gods?
items.explain: Doctors once swore the Hippocratic Oath, promising to do no harm.
items.hook: Hippocrates: illness has **natural** causes, not angry gods.

items.prompt: Which is part of the body’s FIRST line of defence against microbes?

options.text: Skin and stomach acid
Antibodies in the blood
options.feedback: Antibodies come later, from white blood cells.

options.text: Vaccines given as a baby
options.feedback: Vaccines are medicine, not a natural barrier.

items.explain: Skin, mucus, cilia and stomach acid stop most microbes getting in at all.
items.hook: First line = **keep them out**: skin, mucus, cilia and stomach acid.
items.example: A cut needs a plaster because broken skin lets microbes in.

items.prompt: A diet lacking vitamin C causes which disease, once common among sailors?

options.text: Scurvy
Rickets
options.feedback: Rickets is caused by too little vitamin D or calcium.

options.text: Malaria
options.feedback: Malaria is caused by a parasite spread by mosquitoes.

items.explain: Sailors ate citrus fruit (limes) to prevent scurvy.
items.hook: Vitamin **C** for long voyages at **sea**: it prevents scurvy.
items.example: British sailors were nicknamed “limeys” after the lime juice they drank.

items.prompt: Which drug in cigarettes is addictive?
items.explain: Tar causes cancer; carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried in the blood.
items.hook: **Nicotine** hooks you; **tar** causes cancer; **carbon monoxide** steals oxygen.

items.explain: Particles packed in a regular pattern, vibrating in fixed positions.
items.hook: Solid: particles in neat rows, **vibrating on the spot**.
items.example: An ice cube keeps its shape until it starts to melt.

items.explain: Particles far apart, moving fast in all directions.
items.hook: Gas: particles **far apart and zooming** in all directions.
items.example: Air pumped into a bike tyre spreads into every part of it.

items.prompt: Which Greek thinker first suggested that matter is made of tiny pieces that cannot be cut, called atomos?
items.explain: Aristotle disagreed, preferring four elements (earth, water, air, fire), and his idea won for 2000 years.
items.hook: A-tomos = **uncuttable** (Greek): the root of the word atom.

items.prompt: Why does diffusion happen faster in a gas than in a liquid?

options.text: Gas particles move faster with more space
Gas particles are bigger and push harder
options.feedback: The particles are the same; their spacing and speed differ.

options.text: Liquids have no particles to move about
options.feedback: Everything is made of particles.

items.explain: Gas particles move faster and have more space between them. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
items.hook: Diffusion: from **crowded to empty**, faster in gases and faster when hot.
items.example: You can smell toast from upstairs in seconds, but squash takes ages to spread through still water.

items.prompt: When ice melts, what happens to its particles?

options.text: They gain energy and slide past each other
They get bigger, so the ice takes up more room
options.feedback: Particles don’t change size; their arrangement changes.

options.text: They break apart into separate hydrogen and oxygen
options.feedback: They were water molecules all along.

items.explain: They gain energy and can move past each other, but stay close together. A change of state is a physical change: the substance is still water.
items.hook: Melting: particles get enough energy to **slide**, but stay close together.
items.example: Chocolate melts in a hot car and sets again in the fridge: a physical change.

items.prompt: While pure water is boiling, what happens to its temperature?

options.text: It stays at 100 °C until it has all boiled
It keeps rising for as long as you heat it
options.feedback: The energy goes into separating the particles, not raising the temperature.

options.text: It falls as the hottest water escapes as steam
options.feedback: It stays steady.

items.explain: This flat part of a heating curve is why pure substances have sharp boiling points.
items.hook: While water boils, the energy **pulls particles apart** instead of making them hotter.
items.example: Turning the hob up under boiling pasta makes it boil harder, not hotter than 100 °C.

items.prompt: In the myth, Icarus flew too close to the Sun and the wax holding his wings melted. Which change of state is that?

options.text: Solid to liquid
Liquid to gas
options.feedback: That is evaporating or boiling.

options.text: Gas to solid
options.feedback: That is deposition.

items.explain: Melting: the wax particles gained enough energy to slide past each other. (In reality, air gets colder as you climb!)
items.hook: **Melting**: solid → liquid. **Freezing**: liquid → solid.
items.example: Candle wax melts near the flame, and the drips turn solid again as they cool.

items.prompt: What is it called when a solid turns straight into a gas, like dry ice?
items.explain: Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) sublimes at −78 °C.
items.hook: Sublimation **skips the liquid**: solid straight to gas.
items.example: Dry ice is used to make the low, swirling fog on stage at concerts.

items.prompt: What causes the pressure of a gas inside a balloon?
items.explain: Heat it and the particles move faster, hitting harder and more often, so pressure rises.
items.hook: Gas pressure = billions of tiny **particle punches** on the walls every second.
items.example: A football left in hot sun feels harder: its air particles hit the inside faster.

items.hook: Density triangle: **m** on top, **ρ × V** below: density = mass ÷ volume.
items.example: Ice (about 0.92 g/cm³) floats because it is less dense than water (1.0 g/cm³).

items.prompt: Which of these is a compound?

options.text: Water (H₂O)
Oxygen (O₂)
options.feedback: Only one type of atom: an element.

options.text: Air
options.feedback: Air is a mixture of gases, not chemically joined.

options.text: Gold (Au)
options.feedback: Gold is an element.

items.explain: A compound contains two or more different elements chemically bonded.
items.hook: Compound = different atoms **chemically joined**, with a formula like H₂O.
items.example: Water, table salt and carbon dioxide are compounds; oxygen and gold are elements.

items.prompt: How is a mixture different from a compound?

options.text: A mixture’s parts are not chemically joined
A mixture always has a fixed recipe of parts
options.feedback: Compounds have fixed proportions; mixtures can vary.

options.text: A mixture contains only one kind of element
options.feedback: That would be an element.

items.explain: A mixture’s parts are not chemically joined and can be separated physically. Iron and sulfur mixed: a magnet can separate them. Heated together: iron sulfide, a new compound.
items.hook: Mixtures are **just mixed**: you can sort them out without a reaction.
items.example: A magnet pulls iron filings out of sand, but cannot pull the iron out of rust.

items.prompt: Which separation method gets pure water from sea water, by boiling and condensing?
items.explain: The water evaporates and condenses in a cooled tube; the salt stays behind.
items.hook: Distil = **boil, then cool**: the vapour leaves the salt behind.
items.example: Rain is nature’s distillation: the Sun evaporates sea water and leaves the salt behind.

items.prompt: Which method separates the different coloured dyes in an ink?
items.explain: The dyes travel different distances up the paper.
items.hook: Chroma = **colour**, graph = **writing** (Greek): colour-writing.
items.example: Forensic scientists use chromatography to compare the inks on documents.

items.prompt: Which method separates sand from water?
items.explain: Insoluble sand stays on the filter paper.
items.hook: A filter is a **sieve for tiny bits**: insoluble solids stay behind.
items.example: A coffee filter keeps back the grounds and lets the coffee through.

items.prompt: Put the steps for getting salt from rock salt in order.
items.explain: Salt dissolves; sand doesn’t. Filter, then evaporate the water from the solution to leave crystals.
items.hook: Salt dissolves, sand doesn’t: **dissolve, filter, evaporate**.
items.example: Sea salt is made by evaporating sea water in shallow pans.

items.prompt: How many atoms are in one molecule of carbon dioxide, CO₂?
items.explain: One carbon and two oxygens.
items.hook: A small number counts the atom **just before** it: CO₂ = C + O + O.

items.prompt: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
items.explain: Na comes from natrium, its Latin name. Iron is Fe (ferrum), lead Pb (plumbum).
items.hook: Odd symbols come from Latin: **Na**trium (sodium), **Fe**rrum (iron), **Pb** plumbum (lead), **Au**rum (gold).
items.example: Plumbers are named after plumbum, because water pipes were once made of lead.

items.prompt: How can you tell if water is pure?

options.text: It boils at exactly 100 °C
It looks completely clear
options.feedback: Salt water looks clear too.

options.text: It has no taste or smell at all
options.feedback: Never taste-test in a lab!

items.explain: It boils at exactly 100 °C and freezes at exactly 0 °C. Impurities change the melting and boiling points.
items.hook: Pure = **one substance only**, with sharp melting and boiling points.
items.example: Salt is spread on icy roads because it lowers the freezing point of water.

items.prompt: Which Russian chemist published a periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements?
items.explain: He predicted the properties of gallium and germanium before they were found.
items.hook: Mendeleev left **gaps**, and predicted what would fill them.
items.example: Element 101, mendelevium, is named after him.

items.prompt: What do elements in the same group (column) have in common?

options.text: Similar chemical properties
The same atomic mass
options.feedback: Mass increases down a group.

options.text: They are all gases at room temperature
options.feedback: Most groups contain solids.

items.explain: Elements in a group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell.
items.hook: **Groups** go down (columns); **periods** go across (rows).

items.prompt: Group 1 metals, such as sodium and potassium, are called the…
items.explain: They react with water to make an alkaline solution and hydrogen gas.
items.hook: Group 1 metals make **alkalis** with water: hence alkali metals.
items.example: Lithium, the lightest Group 1 metal, is in the battery of your phone.

items.prompt: How does reactivity change going DOWN Group 1?

options.text: It increases
It decreases
options.feedback: Lithium fizzes; caesium explodes.

options.text: It stays the same
options.feedback: There is a clear trend.

items.explain: It increases: potassium reacts more violently than sodium. The outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily.
items.hook: Group 1: reactivity goes **up as you go down**.
items.example: Lithium fizzes gently on water; potassium bursts into lilac flames.

items.prompt: Group 7, including chlorine and iodine, are called the…
items.explain: Halogens are reactive non-metals; reactivity DEcreases down the group.
items.hook: Halogen = **salt-maker** (Greek hals, salt).
items.example: Chlorine keeps swimming pools free of germs; iodine is used as an antiseptic.

items.prompt: Group 0, including helium and neon, are called the…
items.explain: They are very unreactive because their outer shells are full.
items.hook: Noble gases are **snobs**: full outer shells, so they hardly ever react with anyone.
items.example: Neon glows red-orange in signs; helium fills party balloons.

items.prompt: Which property belongs to most NON-metals?

options.text: Poor conductors of heat and electricity
Shiny
options.feedback: Most metals are shiny.

options.text: Malleable (can be hammered into shape)
options.feedback: That is a metal property.

items.explain: Graphite (a form of carbon) is a rare non-metal that conducts electricity.
items.hook: Non-metals are mostly **dull, brittle insulators**; graphite is the rebel that conducts.
items.example: Pencil “lead” is graphite: a thick pencil line on paper can conduct a little electricity.

items.prompt: Where are the metals in the periodic table?

options.text: On the left and in the middle
Only on the far right side
options.feedback: Non-metals are mostly top right.

options.text: Only along the bottom two rows
options.feedback: Most elements are metals.

items.explain: A zig-zag staircase line separates metals from non-metals.
items.hook: Metals on the **left** and middle, non-metals top **right**, split by the staircase.

items.prompt: Which is a CHEMICAL change?

options.text: Burning magnesium
Melting chocolate
options.feedback: That is a physical change of state.

options.text: Dissolving sugar
options.feedback: Dissolving is physical: evaporate the water and the sugar is back.

items.explain: A chemical change makes a new substance and is usually hard to reverse.
items.hook: Chemical change = a **new substance**, usually hard to undo.
items.example: Toast can never turn back into bread, but melted chocolate sets again.

items.prompt: When a fuel such as methane burns completely in oxygen, it makes water and…
items.explain: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen that releases energy. Without enough oxygen, toxic carbon monoxide and soot form.
items.hook: Burning a fuel like methane: fuel + oxygen → **carbon dioxide + water**.
items.example: Gas boilers are checked every year so they burn completely and make no carbon monoxide.

items.prompt: The fire triangle shows a fire needs fuel, oxygen and…

options.text: Heat
Water
options.feedback: Water puts fires out by removing heat.

options.text: Carbon dioxide
options.feedback: CO₂ extinguishers smother fires.

items.explain: Remove any side of the triangle and the fire goes out.
items.hook: Fire triangle: **heat, fuel, oxygen**: take one away and the fire dies.
items.example: A fire blanket cuts off the oxygen from a pan fire.

items.prompt: Magnesium ribbon is burned in a crucible. Its mass INCREASES. Why?

options.text: It has combined with oxygen from the air
Mass was created by the heat of the flame
options.feedback: Mass is never created; the extra came from the air.

options.text: The crucible absorbed some of the magnesium
options.feedback: You weigh the crucible before and after.

items.explain: It has combined with oxygen from the air to make magnesium oxide. Oxidation adds oxygen, so the product is heavier than the metal.
items.hook: The white ash is **heavier** than the ribbon: it has grabbed oxygen from the air.
items.example: Rust weighs more than the iron it came from, because it has gained oxygen (and water).

items.prompt: A reaction that gives out heat, like combustion, is called…

options.text: exothermic
endothermic
options.feedback: Endothermic reactions take in heat and feel cold.

options.text: neutral
options.feedback: That is not a type of energy change.

items.explain: Hand warmers are exothermic; sports cold packs are endothermic.
items.hook: **Ex**othermic: heat **ex**its. **En**dothermic: heat **en**ters.
items.example: A campfire is exothermic; sherbet feels cool as it fizzes on your tongue: endothermic.

items.prompt: Heating copper carbonate breaks it into copper oxide and carbon dioxide. What type of reaction is this?
items.explain: Thermal decomposition: one substance broken down by heat into two or more.
items.hook: Thermal **de-composition**: heat **breaks one substance into two or more**.
items.example: Bicarbonate of soda breaks down when heated, giving off carbon dioxide that helps cakes rise.

items.prompt: Which gas gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint?
items.explain: Oxygen relights a glowing splint; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.
items.hook: Hydrogen **pops**, oxygen **relights** a glowing splint, carbon dioxide turns limewater **milky**.
items.example: The Hindenburg airship was filled with hydrogen, which burned explosively in 1937.

items.hook: Balance with **big numbers in front**; never change the small numbers inside a formula.

items.prompt: What is the pH of a neutral solution, such as pure water?
items.explain: Below 7: acid. Above 7: alkali.
items.hook: pH **7** is neutral: below 7 is acid, above 7 is alkali.
items.example: Lemon juice is about pH 2; soapy water is about pH 9 to 10.

items.prompt: What does an acid react with an alkali to make?

options.text: A salt and water
Hydrogen and oxygen
options.feedback: That is not neutralisation.

options.text: Carbon dioxide only
options.feedback: Carbonates make CO₂ with acids.

items.explain: Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.
items.hook: Acid + alkali → **salt + water**: they cancel each other out.
items.example: Farmers spread lime on acidic fields to neutralise the soil.

items.prompt: Hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → water + which salt?
items.explain: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, sulfuric acid makes sulfates, nitric acid makes nitrates.
items.hook: Hydro**chlor**ic → **chlor**ides, **sulf**uric → **sulf**ates, **nitr**ic → **nitr**ates.
items.example: Sodium chloride is the table salt on your chips.

items.prompt: What gas is made when magnesium reacts with an acid?

options.text: Hydrogen
Oxygen
options.feedback: Test: a squeaky pop means hydrogen.

options.text: Carbon dioxide
options.feedback: That comes from carbonates.

items.explain: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
items.hook: **MASH**: **M**etal + **A**cid → **S**alt + **H**ydrogen.
items.example: Magnesium ribbon fizzes in dilute acid: the bubbles are hydrogen.

items.prompt: Put these metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first.
items.explain: Potassium reacts violently with water; gold doesn’t even react with most acids.
items.hook: Please Stop Calling Me A Careless Zebra Instead Try Learning How Copper Saves Gold: K Na Ca Mg Al C Zn Fe Sn Pb H Cu Ag Au
items.example: Gold coins from old shipwrecks still gleam, while iron cannons from the same wrecks are crusted with rust.

items.prompt: Why is gold found as a pure metal in the ground, while iron must be extracted from ore?

options.text: Gold is too unreactive to combine with others
Gold is much heavier, so it sinks to the surface
options.feedback: It is about reactivity, not mass.

options.text: Iron is rarer, so it is only found in compounds
options.feedback: Iron is far more common than gold.

items.explain: Gold is so unreactive it doesn’t combine with other elements. The least reactive metals (gold, platinum) are found native; even Hephaestus would need a furnace for iron.
items.hook: Gold is the **lazy** metal: too unreactive to join anything, so it lies about pure.
items.example: Gold leaf on old picture frames and church domes still shines after centuries.

items.prompt: An iron nail is dipped in blue copper sulfate solution. It becomes coated in copper. Why?

options.text: Iron is more reactive, so it displaces copper
Copper is more reactive, so it pulls itself out
options.feedback: Then nothing would happen.

options.text: The copper sulfate paints a coat onto the nail
options.feedback: It is a displacement reaction.

items.explain: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the compound. A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of its compound.
items.hook: Displacement is a **playground bully**: the more reactive metal pushes the weaker one out.

items.prompt: Indigestion tablets neutralise excess stomach acid. Are they acids or bases?
items.explain: They contain bases such as calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide.
items.hook: Bases **cancel** acids: that is neutralisation.
items.example: Many indigestion tablets contain calcium carbonate, the same compound as chalk.

items.prompt: Universal indicator turns which colour in a strong acid?
items.explain: Red/orange for acids, green for neutral, blue/purple for alkalis.
items.hook: Universal indicator runs like a **rainbow**: red (strong acid) → green (neutral) → purple (strong alkali).
items.example: Red cabbage juice is a homemade indicator: pink in vinegar, blue or green in alkalis.

items.prompt: How is igneous rock formed?

options.text: Molten rock cools and solidifies
Layers of sediment are pressed together
options.feedback: That is sedimentary rock.

options.text: Heat and pressure change other rocks
options.feedback: That is metamorphic rock.

items.explain: When molten rock (magma or lava) cools and solidifies. Granite cools slowly underground (big crystals); basalt cools fast at the surface (small crystals).
items.hook: Igneous comes from Latin ignis, **fire**: it starts as molten rock.
items.example: The Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland is columns of basalt from cooled lava.

items.prompt: In which type of rock are fossils usually found?
items.explain: Sediment buries remains gently; heat and melting destroy fossils.
items.hook: Fossils rest in **sedimentary** rock, laid down gently in layers like pages in a book.
items.example: Fossil hunters find ammonites on the beach at Lyme Regis.

items.prompt: Marble is metamorphic rock formed from which sedimentary rock?
items.explain: Heat and pressure recrystallise limestone into marble; the Parthenon in Athens is built of marble.
items.hook: Meta-morph = **change of form** (Greek): limestone changes into marble.
items.example: Michelangelo’s statue of David is carved from marble.

items.prompt: About how much of today’s air is nitrogen?

options.text: About 78%
About 21%
options.feedback: That is oxygen.

options.text: About 1%
options.feedback: That is roughly argon.

items.explain: Nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon about 0.9%, carbon dioxide about 0.04%.
items.hook: Air is about **four-fifths nitrogen** and one-fifth oxygen.

items.prompt: Which of these REMOVES carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?

options.text: Photosynthesis
Burning fossil fuels
options.feedback: That adds CO₂.

options.text: Respiration
options.feedback: Respiration releases CO₂.

items.explain: Plants, algae and the oceans absorb carbon dioxide.
items.hook: Plants are carbon **sponges**: photosynthesis takes CO₂ out of the air.
items.example: Planting new forests is one way countries try to soak up carbon dioxide.

items.prompt: How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?

options.text: They absorb heat from the Earth and re-emit it
They make a hole in the ozone layer that lets heat in
options.feedback: The ozone hole is a different problem.

options.text: They reflect extra sunlight down onto the surface
options.feedback: Greenhouse gases let most sunlight through; they absorb and re-emit heat radiated by the Earth.

items.explain: They absorb heat radiated from the Earth’s surface and re-emit it, trapping it in the atmosphere. More CO₂ and methane mean more heat trapped: the enhanced greenhouse effect.
items.hook: Greenhouse gases are a **blanket**: the heat gets out more slowly.
items.example: Venus, with its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere, is hotter than Mercury, though further from the Sun.

items.prompt: Put this route of a carbon atom in order.
items.explain: Carbon cycles between the air, living things, oceans and rocks.
items.hook: Carbon goes **round and round**: air → plants → animals → air.
items.example: The carbon in your toast was carbon dioxide in the air only months ago.

items.prompt: The breaking down of rocks by rain, ice and plants without them moving is called…
items.explain: Erosion is when the bits are carried away; freeze–thaw weathering splits rocks as water freezes and expands.
items.hook: **Weathering** breaks rock where it is; **erosion** carries the bits away.
items.example: Potholes grow in winter as water in cracks freezes and expands.

items.prompt: A car travels at a steady 30 mph in a straight line. What can you say about the forces on it?

options.text: They are balanced
The driving force is bigger
options.feedback: Then it would speed up.

options.text: There are no forces acting on it
options.feedback: Friction and air resistance act all the time.

items.explain: They are balanced: driving force equals resistive forces. Balanced forces mean no change in motion: steady speed or stationary (Newton’s first law).
items.hook: Balanced = **no change**: still stays still, moving keeps moving steadily.
items.example: If a car stops suddenly your body keeps moving forward: that is why seatbelts matter.

items.prompt: Why does a skydiver reach a terminal velocity?

options.text: Air resistance rises until it equals weight
Gravity switches off once you fall fast enough
options.feedback: Gravity keeps pulling.

options.text: The parachute is open from the moment you jump
options.feedback: Terminal velocity happens with or without a parachute.

items.explain: Air resistance grows with speed until it equals weight, so forces balance. With the parachute open, a much bigger air resistance gives a slower terminal velocity.
items.hook: Terminal = **end** (Latin terminus): the top speed, when air resistance equals weight.
items.example: Skydivers fall at about 55 m/s spread flat, but much faster diving head-down.

items.prompt: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength. On Earth g ≈ 10 N/kg. What does a 50 kg person weigh, in newtons?
items.explain: 50 × 10 = 500 N. On the Moon (g ≈ 1.6 N/kg) the same person would weigh only about 80 N.
items.hook: Weight = mass × g: **W = mg**, with g ≈ 10 N/kg on Earth.
items.example: A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 10 N.

items.prompt: What happens to your MASS if you travel to the Moon?

options.text: It stays the same
It falls to about a sixth
options.feedback: That is your weight.

options.text: It becomes zero in space
options.feedback: Mass is the amount of matter in you.

items.explain: It stays the same; only your weight changes, to about a sixth. Mass is measured in kg; weight is a force, in newtons.
items.hook: Mass is the **stuff** in you; weight is the **pull** on that stuff.
items.example: Astronauts bounded about on the Moon in heavy suits because they weighed only a sixth as much.

items.prompt: On a distance–time graph, what does a horizontal line mean?

options.text: The object is stationary
It is moving at a steady speed
options.feedback: A steady speed is a straight sloping line.

options.text: It is accelerating
options.feedback: Accelerating gives a curve getting steeper.

items.explain: The gradient of a distance–time graph is the speed.
items.hook: Distance–time: a flat line = **stopped**; a steeper line = **faster**.
items.example: On a graph of a bus journey, each flat bit is a stop at a bus stop.

items.prompt: Atlas holds up the sky. The sky pushes down on Atlas. By Newton’s third law, how do these two forces compare?

options.text: Equal in size, opposite in direction
The sky’s push is bigger, so Atlas strains
options.feedback: Interaction pairs are always equal.

options.text: Atlas’s push is bigger, so the sky stays up
options.feedback: Interaction pairs are always equal, whatever is happening.

items.explain: They are equal in size and opposite in direction. For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; the pair acts on different objects.
items.hook: Newton 3: **every push gets a push back**, equal and opposite, on the other object.
items.example: A swimmer pushes the water backwards, and the water pushes the swimmer forwards.

items.hook: Formula triangle: **d** on top, **s × t** below: speed = distance ÷ time.
items.example: A sprinter running 100 m in 10 s averages 10 m/s.

items.hook: Formula triangle: **F** on top, **p × A** below: pressure = force ÷ area.
items.example: A sharp knife cuts easily: its tiny edge area gives a huge pressure.

items.hook: Moment = force × distance: a **longer spanner** turns a nut more easily.
items.example: Door handles are far from the hinges, so a small push gives a big turning effect.

items.prompt: Hooke’s law says the extension of a spring is proportional to the…
items.explain: Double the force, double the stretch, until the limit of proportionality.
items.hook: Hooke’s law: **double the pull, double the stretch** (up to the limit).
items.example: Spring luggage scales use Hooke’s law to weigh your suitcase.

items.prompt: A drawn bow is about to fire an arrow. Which energy store is full?

options.text: Elastic potential
Gravitational potential
options.feedback: That is for height.

options.text: Nuclear
options.feedback: Nuclear energy is stored in atomic nuclei.

items.explain: Released, the elastic store empties into the arrow’s kinetic store.
items.hook: Stretched, squashed or bent = an **elastic** store.
items.example: A trampoline’s springs store elastic energy and fling you back up.

items.prompt: What does the law of conservation of energy say?

options.text: Energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred
We should always switch off lights we are not using
options.feedback: That is energy saving, not the law.

options.text: Energy gets used up and disappears when things move
options.feedback: It is transferred, often to thermal energy.

items.explain: The total is always the same; wasted energy usually ends up warming the surroundings.
items.hook: Energy is like **money moved between accounts**: the total never changes.
items.example: An old filament bulb gets hot: much of its energy is wasted heating the room.

items.prompt: Why does a dropped ball bounce lower each time?

options.text: Some energy is transferred to heat and sound
Some energy is destroyed at every bounce
options.feedback: Energy is never destroyed.

options.text: Gravity gets stronger as the ball slows down
options.feedback: g stays the same.

items.explain: Some energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat and sound at each bounce. Less energy remains in the ball’s gravitational store at the top of each bounce.
items.hook: Every bounce **leaks** a little energy as heat and sound.
items.example: Squash players warm the ball up before a game, because a warm ball bounces higher.

items.prompt: Which is a RENEWABLE energy resource?

options.text: Wind
Coal
options.feedback: Fossil fuels took millions of years to form.

options.text: Natural gas
options.feedback: A fossil fuel.

options.text: Uranium
options.feedback: Nuclear fuel will run out.

items.explain: Renewables (wind, solar, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biofuel) will not run out.
items.hook: **Renew**able resources **renew** themselves: wind, sun, waves, tides, rivers.
items.example: Solar panels on roofs and wind farms in the North Sea.

items.prompt: Why do saucepans have metal bases but plastic handles?

options.text: Metal conducts heat; plastic insulates
Plastic is stronger and lasts much longer
options.feedback: It is about conducting heat.

options.text: Metal is cheaper and easier to shape
options.feedback: The reason is conduction.

items.explain: Metal is a good thermal conductor; plastic is an insulator. Thermal energy is transferred by conduction, convection and radiation.
items.hook: Metals **pass heat on**; plastic and wood **hold it back**.
items.example: A metal spoon left in hot tea soon gets too hot to hold.

items.prompt: Warm air rises above a radiator and cool air sinks to replace it. What is this transfer called?
items.explain: Convection currents happen in liquids and gases, because warm fluid is less dense.
items.hook: Convection: hot fluid **rises**, cool fluid **sinks**, round and round.
items.example: A hot-air balloon rises because the air inside is warmer and less dense.

items.hook: Power = energy ÷ time: a 3 kW kettle transfers **3000 J every second**.
items.example: Electricity bills count kilowatt-hours: 1 kW running for 1 hour.

items.prompt: You add a second bulb in SERIES. What happens to the brightness?

options.text: Both bulbs are dimmer
Both bulbs are brighter
options.feedback: More resistance means less current.

options.text: No change in brightness
options.feedback: The current falls.

items.explain: Both bulbs are dimmer than one bulb alone. Total resistance goes up, so current goes down. In parallel, each bulb stays as bright as one alone.
items.hook: Series = **one road**: more bulbs share the push, so each is dimmer.
items.example: In old Christmas lights wired in series, one broken bulb blacked out the whole string.

items.prompt: Why are house lights wired in PARALLEL?

options.text: Each light gets full voltage and its own switch
It uses less wire, so it is cheaper to install
options.feedback: The reason is independence and full voltage.

options.text: It makes the bulbs last much longer before failing
options.feedback: Not the main reason.

items.explain: Each light gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off separately. If one bulb fails in parallel, the others stay on.
items.hook: Parallel = **own branch, full voltage** for each.
items.example: You can switch off the kitchen light without the hall light going out.

items.prompt: Which meter measures current, and how is it connected?
items.explain: Voltmeters go in parallel across a component.
items.hook: An ammeter must **join the queue** (series) to count the charge going past; a voltmeter watches from the side.

items.prompt: What is the unit of resistance?
items.explain: Symbol Ω. Named after Georg Ohm.
items.hook: The ohm’s symbol, Ω, is the Greek capital **omega**.

items.prompt: A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall. Why?

options.text: Rubbing moves electrons, charging the balloon
The balloon becomes magnetic when it is rubbed
options.feedback: It is static electricity, not magnetism.

options.text: Rubbing leaves a sticky layer of hair oil on it
options.feedback: It is electric charge.

items.explain: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract. The Greeks noticed amber (ēlektron) does this when rubbed!
items.hook: Rubbing **moves electrons**. Like charges repel; opposites attract.
items.example: You can get a small shock from a car door after sliding across the seat.

items.prompt: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?

options.text: More turns, more current, an iron core
Fewer turns of wire and a plastic core
options.feedback: An iron core concentrates the field.

options.text: Less current and a copper core inside
options.feedback: More current makes a stronger field.

items.explain: More turns of wire, more current, and an iron core. Electromagnets can be switched off, which is why scrapyard cranes use them.
items.hook: Stronger electromagnet: more **turns**, more **current**, an iron **core**.
items.example: Electric door locks and doorbells use electromagnets.

items.prompt: Outside a bar magnet, field lines go from…

options.text: north to south
south to north
options.feedback: The convention is north to south outside the magnet.

options.text: the middle outwards to both ends
options.feedback: They start at N and end at S.

items.explain: The north pole to the south pole. The closer the lines, the stronger the field.
items.hook: Outside a magnet, field lines run **north → south**, the way a compass needle points.
items.example: Iron filings sprinkled round a magnet show its field-line pattern.

items.hook: Formula triangle: **V** on top, **I × R** below: V = IR.
items.example: Phone chargers are labelled with volts and amps, such as 5 V, 2 A.

items.prompt: Why can’t sound travel through space?

options.text: No particles to pass on the vibrations
It is far too cold for sound to move
options.feedback: Temperature isn’t the reason.

options.text: Space is too big, so the sound fades out
options.feedback: Sound needs a medium; space is a vacuum.

items.explain: Sound is a longitudinal wave of vibrating particles.
items.hook: Sound is a **passed-on wobble**: no particles, nothing to pass it on.
items.example: Astronauts on spacewalks talk by radio, which can cross empty space.

items.prompt: A higher pitched note has a…

options.text: higher frequency
larger amplitude
options.feedback: Amplitude affects loudness.

options.text: lower frequency
options.feedback: Lower frequency gives a lower pitch.

items.explain: Frequency (Hz) is the number of waves per second.
items.hook: **Hi**gh frequency = **hi**gh pitch; bigger amplitude = louder.
items.example: A flute plays higher notes than a tuba: its sound waves have a higher frequency.

items.prompt: When light reflects off a mirror, how do the angles compare?

options.text: Incidence equals reflection
Reflection is always 90°
options.feedback: The two angles, measured from the normal, are always equal; light hitting along the normal bounces straight back.

options.text: The reflected angle is double
options.feedback: They are equal.

items.explain: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal, a line at 90° to the mirror.
items.hook: Angle in = angle out, both measured from the **normal**.
items.example: Snooker players use the same rule to bounce a ball off the cushion.

items.prompt: A straw in water looks bent. Why?

options.text: Light changes speed and direction (refraction)
The water bends the straw as it soaks in
options.feedback: The straw is straight.

options.text: Light reflects off the surface of the water
options.feedback: It is refraction.

items.explain: Light changes speed and direction as it passes from water to air (refraction). Light slows down in denser materials like water and glass.
items.hook: Refraction = **bending** as light changes speed.
items.example: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is.

items.prompt: White light passes through a prism and splits into a spectrum. What does this show?

options.text: White light is a mixture of colours
The prism adds colour to the light
options.feedback: Newton showed a second prism can recombine the colours.

options.text: Light is made of seven separate rays
options.feedback: The spectrum is continuous; “seven colours” is just how Newton named the bands.

items.explain: This is dispersion: each colour refracts by a different amount.
items.hook: **R**ichard **O**f **Y**ork **G**ave **B**attle **I**n **V**ain: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
items.example: A rainbow is sunlight split into colours by raindrops.

items.prompt: Why does a red apple look red in white light?

options.text: It reflects red and absorbs the rest
It gives out its own red light
options.feedback: It is not a light source.

options.text: It absorbs red light and reflects the rest
options.feedback: It reflects red.

items.explain: It reflects red light and absorbs the other colours. In blue light, the same apple would look black.
items.hook: You see the colour that is **bounced back**; all the others are absorbed.
items.example: A black T-shirt gets hot in the sun because it absorbs every colour.

items.prompt: Which travels faster: light or sound?
items.explain: Light: about 300 000 km/s. Sound in air: about 340 m/s.
items.hook: Lightning: **flash first, crash later**. Light wins every race.
items.example: Count the seconds from flash to thunder: about 3 seconds for every kilometre.

items.hook: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength: **v = fλ**.
items.example: On a pond, count the ripples passing each second and measure the gap between crests.

items.prompt: What causes the seasons?

options.text: The Earth’s tilted axis
The Earth getting closer to the Sun in summer
options.feedback: The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.

options.text: The Sun burning hotter for half of the year
options.feedback: The Sun’s output is almost constant.

items.explain: The Earth’s axis is tilted, so each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year. When the northern hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, days are longer and sunlight is more direct: summer.
items.hook: It is the **tilt** (about 23.5°): each hemisphere takes a turn leaning towards the Sun.
items.example: When it is summer in Britain it is winter in Australia.

items.prompt: What keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?

options.text: Gravity
Magnetism
options.feedback: Gravity holds orbits together.

options.text: The Sun’s light
options.feedback: Light does not hold things in orbit.

items.explain: Gravity pulls the Moon towards the Earth, constantly curving its path into an orbit.
items.hook: The Moon is **always falling** towards Earth, but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing.
items.example: The Moon’s gravity also pulls on the oceans, causing the tides.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon have phases?

options.text: We see different amounts of its lit half
The Earth’s shadow covers part of it each night
options.feedback: That is an eclipse, which is rare.

options.text: It grows and shrinks in size as it orbits
options.feedback: It stays the same size.
